subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Prove that the area of the triangle formed by the tangents at (x₁,y₁), (x₂,y₂), (x₃,y₃) to the parabola y² = 4ax is (1/16a)|(y₁−y₂)(y₂−y₃)(y₃−y₁)| square units.

mark_split.label: Write the tangent at each point and find the pairwise intersections
Set up the area determinant and factor it
Convert to y-differences and write the boxed area

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Maths-2B, book p.25 — LAQ chapter 2 Parabola, answer 15, on the same Super Scoring Page (SSP 25) as answer 14, with the printed aside 'VERY EASY METHOD'. Printed appearances: AP 2018, TS 2015. One of the chapter's Five STAR Q's. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS — no margin mark tags are printed; the split follows the proof's stages. NOTATION: like answer 14, the book's own working passes through a 2×2 determinant of coordinate differences; one line is typeset here with render:katex for the same reason. No two-book union check was possible for Maths-2B (no second-year TSBIE Basic Learning Material is on hand), and no board back-test beyond diffing against this book's own five Guess Papers.

steps.label: Find the pairwise tangent intersections
steps.margin_note: Three marks for all three intersection points — the biggest single step of the proof.
lines: Let D(at₁²,2at₁), E(at₂²,2at₂), F(at₃²,2at₃) be the three points on y² = 4ax.
The tangent at parameter t is ty = x + at²; so at D, E, F: t₁y=x+at₁² …(1), t₂y=x+at₂² …(2), t₃y=x+at₃² …(3)
(1) − (2): (t₁−t₂)y = a(t₁²−t₂²) ⇒ y = a(t₁+t₂); from (1), x = t₁y − at₁² = at₁t₂
So the tangents at D, E meet at P = (at₁t₂, a(t₁+t₂)); similarly Q = (at₂t₃, a(t₂+t₃)), R = (at₃t₁, a(t₃+t₁))
steps.why: Every tangent to y² = 4ax at parameter t has the same shape ty = x + at², so subtracting two such equations cancels x immediately and gives y directly, which is the fastest way to the two tangents' meeting point.
common_mistakes: Using the point form of the tangent (yy₁=2a(x+x₁)) instead of the parameter form, which makes the elimination far harder.
Mixing up which pair of tangents meets at which of P, Q, R.
steps.memory_tip: The tangent at parameter t is always ty = x + at² — subtract two of these and x cancels, handing over y first.

steps.label: Set up and factor the area determinant
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Half of this determinant's work was already done when P, Q, R were written down in step 1.

lines.text: \text{Area of }\triangle PQR = \frac{1}{2}\begin{vmatrix} x_1-x_2 & x_1-x_3 \\ y_1-y_2 & y_1-y_3 \end{vmatrix}

lines: x₁−x₂ = at₁t₂−at₂t₃ = at₂(t₁−t₃); x₁−x₃ = at₁t₂−at₃t₁ = at₁(t₂−t₃)
steps.why: Each coordinate difference of P, Q, R factors neatly because P, Q, R were themselves built from t₁, t₂, t₃ — substituting those factored forms into the determinant leaves one common factor (t₁−t₃)(t₂−t₃) that can be pulled straight out.
common_mistakes: Re-deriving x₁−x₂ etc. from scratch by expanding the coordinates instead of factoring them directly.
Losing the sign in the final factoring, which flips (t₂−t₁) to (t₁−t₂).
steps.memory_tip: P, Q, R were built from products and sums of t₁, t₂, t₃ — their differences factor the same way column by column.

steps.label: Convert to y-differences and write the boxed area
steps.margin_note: Last two marks. Compare the denominator with answer 14's — 16a here, not 8a, because of the extra 1/2.
steps.why: This area comes out to exactly half of answer 14's area for the same three parameters, because the extra factor of 1/2 sitting in front of the determinant here has no counterpart in the earlier proof — that is also why the denominator here is 16a instead of 8a.
common_mistakes: Reusing answer 14's final denominator of 8a instead of the 16a that the extra 1/2 here produces.
Dropping the absolute value bars again, the same slip as in answer 14.
steps.memory_tip: This triangle (from tangents) is always half the area of the triangle in answer 14 (from the points themselves) for the same three parameters — 16a instead of 8a.

insider_note: This proof and answer 14's share almost every line — the only real difference is the extra 1/2 in front of the determinant here, which is exactly why the final denominator doubles from 8a to 16a.
